title: Ridgeline Custom Builds x Ghostbird Content Interview

summary.short_summary: Desmond is running five custom home builds and two phased renovations at once, including a new ~11,000 sq ft mountain home referred by a client from four years ago. He retold a story about personally, and for free, fixing a drainage-related basement issue for a young couple over a year after their build closed, tying it to his late father's framing-trade philosophy: 'measure the relationship, not just the lumber.' He also broke down the difference between design-build and hiring a separate architect and builder, and shared a lighter story about coaching his son's rec league basketball team.

sentences.text: Hey Desmond, how's build season treating you?
Busy in the good way. We've got five custom homes going right now plus two phased renovations.
Five at once, that's a lot of moving pieces.
It is, but we finally have a project manager handling two of them full time, which has honestly saved my sanity this year.
Good, let's talk business first, then I want to get into a couple stories. Anything big land recently?
Yeah, we just picked up a large mountain home project, about eleven thousand square feet, up near the ski resort area. Came from a referral.
Who referred them?
Actually a client from four years ago, a family we built a fairly modest four-bedroom for. Small world.
Speaking of past clients, I remember you mentioning something once about doing a repair for a client years after a project closed, for free. Can you tell me that whole story?

Yeah, so, this was maybe six years ago. A young couple, first home we ever built for them, and about a year and a half after closing, their basement had a small water issue during a really heavy spring melt.

It technically wasn't our fault, it was a landscaping drainage issue on their end that had nothing to do with our build. But I went out myself on a Saturday and just fixed it. Didn't charge them a dime.
Why?

Honestly, my dad drilled this into me. He was a framer his whole life, and he used to say measure the relationship, not just the lumber. Meaning, the invoice ends, but the relationship with that family doesn't have to.
Did that couple ever come back?

That's the thing, that same couple has now referred us to five different families over the years. That mountain home I just mentioned, actually, is a referral that traces back to them two people removed.
Okay, that story practically writes itself. Measure the relationship, not the lumber is such a strong line, we're using that as the hook.
My dad would get a kick out of that if he saw it on the internet.
Is he still around?
He is, retired now, but he still shows up on job sites sometimes just to make sure I haven't gotten sloppy, his words.

That's great, we might use that detail too. Okay, switching gears, I know you've talked before about design-build versus hiring a separate architect. Walk me through that again for people who don't know the difference.

Sure. When a client hires an architect separately from their builder, they're essentially the general contractor between those two parties whether they realize it or not. If the design and the build don't line up perfectly, arguments happen, and the client is stuck in the middle deciding who's right.
And with design-build?

With design-build, it's one team, one contract, one point of accountability. If something doesn't work structurally, we catch it in-house before it ever gets built, instead of after the framing's already up.
Does that save money too, or mostly headaches?
Both, honestly. I'd say most of our clients save somewhere in the range of ten to fifteen percent versus the separate-architect route, just from avoiding change orders caused by miscommunication.
Okay, that's a really clean, useful post for anyone considering building. Last thing, anything going on outside of work?
I've been coaching my son's rec league basketball team on Saturday mornings. Nine and ten year olds, so mostly just chaos.
Any good stories from that?
One kid on the team never wants to shoot, too scared to miss in front of everyone. Took me like six weeks to get him to take one real shot in a game.
Did he make it?
Airball, completely missed everything, backboard and all. But the whole team cheered like he won the championship, and he had the biggest smile I've seen all season.
That's such a good one, and honestly ties right back into the client relationship stuff, showing up for people even when the outcome isn't perfect.
Never thought about it that way, but yeah, that tracks.
Okay, so today I've got the measure the relationship story, the design-build versus separate architect breakdown, and the basketball airball story. I'll get you drafts by early next week.
Sounds good. I'll have my site super send over updated photos from the mountain home project too, might be useful for one of these.
Perfect, that'll help a lot. Thanks Desmond, talk soon.
Thanks Ryan, take care.
